Visium - Guided Clustering Tutorial

Compiled: October 26, 2026

From unnormalized counts to UMAP for Visium v1/v2 and HD

Independent learning notes, following the teaching structure and pkgdown / Flatly presentation of the Seurat PBMC3k tutorial. Real v1/v2 results are distinguished from HD code templates.

Set up the Seurat object#

In this tutorial, we will analyze spatial gene expression data generated with Visium v1, Visium v2/CytAssist, and Visium HD. We begin with unnormalized gene counts and work through quality control, normalization, feature selection, PCA, graph-based clustering, and UMAP. We then display the same clusters on the tissue image.

The central workflow is similar to the PBMC3k analysis. The important difference is what each column of the matrix represents. A conventional Visium column represents a spot, an HD binned column represents a spatial bin, and a segmentation-derived column represents an inferred cell. A spot or bin should not automatically be interpreted as a single cell.2, 3, 4

Here, v1/v2 identify the experimental workflows represented by our examples. They are not Space Ranger software versions or Seurat image-class selectors.

DatasetObservation represented by one columnWorkflow used here
Visium v1 / v2A tissue-associated spot, often containing several cellsStandard preprocessing and clustering
Visium HD, binnedAn 8 µm bin; 2 and 16 µm are other available resolutionsLog-normalization, sketch clustering, full-data projection
Visium HD, segmentedA segmentation-derived cell associated with a polygonStandard clustering, with cell- and segmentation-specific QC

We use the log-normalization route in the main example so that each step corresponds closely to the PBMC3k tutorial. This is a teaching workflow, not a claim that one normalization method is optimal for every tissue or assay. An alternative SCTransform route is provided separately.

What does “raw counts” mean here? The file filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5 still contains unnormalized counts. “Filtered” refers to the upstream selection of tissue-associated barcodes (and applicable feature filtering), not Seurat normalization. We do not need to start from the file named raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5, which also contains background barcodes.6

The v1/v2 figures below were generated for this tutorial using two public mouse brain datasets. The HD sections provide complete, separately labeled workflows for your own Space Ranger outputs; their results have not been fabricated or substituted with single-cell data.

library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(42)
packageVersion("Seurat")
packageVersion("SeuratObject")

The executed examples use Seurat 5.5.1 and SeuratObject 5.4.0. Basic HD bin import requires Seurat ≥5.1.0; segmented-cell import requires Seurat ≥5.4.0 and SeuratObject ≥5.3.0. H5 input uses hdf5r; HD Parquet input additionally requires arrow, and polygon workflows require their spatial dependencies.5, 4

Load the example datasets#

For the first example, we use a sagittal-anterior mouse brain section generated with Visium v1. For the second, we use a coronal mouse brain FFPE section processed with CytAssist. The expression H5 and spatial archive are available from the corresponding 10x dataset pages: v1 dataset and v2 dataset. Together, these four downloads are approximately 76 MB.7, 8

We keep each H5 file beside its spatial/ directory. These are already Space Ranger outputs; we do not rerun FASTQ processing in this tutorial.

download_visium <- function(prefix, data.dir) {
  dir.create(data.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  download.file(
    paste0(prefix, "filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5"),
    destfile = file.path(data.dir, "filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5"),
    mode = "wb"
  )
  spatial.tar <- file.path(data.dir, "spatial.tar.gz")
  download.file(paste0(prefix, "spatial.tar.gz"), spatial.tar, mode = "wb")
  untar(spatial.tar, exdir = data.dir)
}

v1.prefix <- paste0(
  "https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/spatial-exp/1.0.0/",
  "V1_Mouse_Brain_Sagittal_Anterior/V1_Mouse_Brain_Sagittal_Anterior_"
)
v2.prefix <- paste0(
  "https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/spatial-exp/2.0.0/",
  "CytAssist_FFPE_Mouse_Brain_Rep1/CytAssist_FFPE_Mouse_Brain_Rep1_"
)

# Skip these downloads if the files are already available locally.
download_visium(v1.prefix, "data/visium_v1")
download_visium(v2.prefix, "data/visium_v2")

We read the matrix, image, scale factors, and spatial coordinates together using Load10X_Spatial(). Reading only the matrix with Read10X_h5() would omit the spatial information.5

v1 <- Load10X_Spatial(
  data.dir = "data/visium_v1",
  filename = "filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5",
  assay = "Spatial", slice = "v1", filter.matrix = TRUE
)
v2 <- Load10X_Spatial(
  data.dir = "data/visium_v2",
  filename = "filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5",
  assay = "Spatial", slice = "v2", filter.matrix = TRUE
)

# We begin with v1, then repeat the same workflow on v2.
visium <- v1
DefaultAssay(visium) <- "Spatial"
visium
## An object of class Seurat 
## 31053 features across 2696 samples within 1 assay 
## Active assay: Spatial (31053 features, 0 variable features)
##  1 layer present: counts
##  1 spatial field of view present: v1

We can inspect a small part of the count matrix. Rows represent genes, columns represent spots, and the values represent molecule counts. The dots in this sparse matrix indicate zeros.

counts <- GetAssayData(visium, assay = "Spatial", layer = "counts")
counts[1:5, 1:6]
Images(visium)
head(visium[[]])

## Xkr4                     .                  .                  .

Seurat sometimes uses the word “cells” in accessors and object summaries. In this section those identifiers refer to spots. We avoid converting the full count matrix to a dense matrix.

QC and selecting spots for further analysis#

We start by examining the total count per spot (nCount_Spatial) and the number of detected genes (nFeature_Spatial). These values are calculated from the original counts. We inspect the distributions and their spatial locations together, since RNA content can change with tissue anatomy and cellular density.

VlnPlot(
  visium,
  features = c("nCount_Spatial", "nFeature_Spatial"),
  pt.size = 0, ncol = 2
)

SpatialFeaturePlot(
  visium, features = "nCount_Spatial", images = "v1"
)

The PBMC3k thresholds are not general Visium thresholds. A spot with many detected genes may contain more cells, rather than being a droplet doublet. Conversely, a low-count tissue region may be biologically meaningful. Review the tissue mask, image alignment, and sample-specific distributions before applying stronger filters.2, 6

Mitochondrial proportions may be useful, but only if the relevant genes are represented and named appropriately. Human symbols often begin with MT-, whereas mouse symbols often begin with mt-. Probe coverage and gene identifiers must be checked before interpreting this metric.15

mt.features <- grep("^(MT-|mt-)", rownames(visium[["Spatial"]]), value = TRUE)
if (length(mt.features) > 0L) {
  visium[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(
    visium, features = mt.features, assay = "Spatial"
  )
  VlnPlot(visium, features = "percent.mt", pt.size = 0)
  SpatialFeaturePlot(visium, features = "percent.mt", images = "v1")
}

For the executed teaching examples, we retain all tissue-associated spots with nonzero information. The setting below is a technical exclusion only; it is not a complete biological QC policy. Set a more restrictive threshold only after reviewing your own sample.

min.features <- 1L
visium$qc_keep <- (
  visium$nCount_Spatial > 0 &
  visium$nFeature_Spatial >= min.features
)

table(visium$qc_keep)
SpatialDimPlot(visium, images = "v1", group.by = "qc_keep")
visium <- subset(visium, subset = qc_keep)

In the executed v1 example, 2,696 spots were retained. Before filtering another dataset, examine which locations would be removed and document the chosen criteria.

Normalizing the data#

We next normalize the counts so that differences in total detected molecules do not dominate subsequent analysis. Here we use LogNormalize: each spot is scaled by its total count, multiplied by 10,000, and log-transformed. The original counts remain in the counts layer; normalized values are stored in the data layer.18

visium <- NormalizeData(
  visium,
  assay = "Spatial",
  normalization.method = "LogNormalize",
  scale.factor = 10000
)

This keeps the steps visible and comparable to the single-cell tutorial. In spatial data, count depth can reflect both technical effects and genuine differences in local cell density. Consider how normalization affects the biological question rather than assuming that every difference in depth is unwanted.

Alternative: use SCTransform for the standard Visium branch

The Seurat spatial vignette also demonstrates SCTransform. It replaces the three operations NormalizeData(), FindVariableFeatures(), and ScaleData(). If you choose this route, begin from a QC-filtered count object and run the following block, including its PCA on the SCT assay. Then rejoin at Determine the dimensionality of the dataset, skipping the main-route feature-selection, scaling, and PCA blocks. Do not run both normalization routes in sequence.9

# Alternative branch: run on a QC-filtered counts object.
visium <- SCTransform(
  visium, assay = "Spatial", new.assay.name = "SCT",
  vst.flavor = "v2", verbose = FALSE
)
DefaultAssay(visium) <- "SCT"
visium <- RunPCA(visium, assay = "SCT", npcs = 50, seed.use = 42)
# Continue with PCA diagnostics, neighbors, clustering, and UMAP.
# Skip the main-route feature-selection and scaling blocks below.

The figures in the main tutorial use LogNormalize, not this alternative branch.

Identification of highly variable features#

We identify genes with substantial variation across spots and use them to build a lower-dimensional representation. Restricting PCA to informative features reduces the contribution of genes that carry little variation in this dataset.19

visium <- FindVariableFeatures(
  visium,
  assay = "Spatial",
  selection.method = "vst",
  nfeatures = 2000
)

head(VariableFeatures(visium), 10)
VariableFeaturePlot(visium)

The selected genes are analytical features, not automatically marker genes for a particular cell type. Different panels and capture chemistries may expose different sets of measurable genes.

Scaling the data#

Before PCA, we center and scale the selected genes across spots. We scale only the variable features used below, which avoids creating an unnecessary dense matrix for every gene. This operation creates the scale.data layer; it does not overwrite the original counts.20

visium <- ScaleData(
  visium,
  assay = "Spatial",
  features = VariableFeatures(visium)
)

We do not automatically regress out mitochondrial proportion or total counts. Whether a covariate should be removed depends on the assay and the question, particularly when it also reflects anatomical differences.

Perform linear dimensional reduction#

We run PCA on the scaled variable features. Each spot is now represented by a smaller number of expression-derived coordinates. These are not its tissue coordinates: a principal component describes an expression pattern, whereas the image contains physical positions.21

visium <- RunPCA(
  visium,
  assay = "Spatial",
  features = VariableFeatures(visium),
  npcs = 50,
  seed.use = 42
)

print(visium[["pca"]], dims = 1:5, nfeatures = 5)
DimHeatmap(visium, dims = 1:6, cells = 500, balanced = TRUE)

Inspect the genes and patterns contributing to early PCs. Strong gradients in technical metrics, tissue damage, or an incorrectly included background region should be understood before interpreting the resulting groups.

Determine the dimensionality of the dataset#

We use an elbow plot as one diagnostic for choosing the number of PCs. There is no universal cutoff that applies to every tissue, assay, or bin size. The value below is a reproducible starting choice for these examples, not an optimized parameter for an unseen sample.

ElbowPlot(visium, ndims = 50)
dims.use <- 1:30

Cluster the spots#

We construct a nearest-neighbor graph using the selected PCs and identify communities in that graph. The resolution parameter controls the granularity of the partition. We use 0.5 here and retain the resulting labels in seurat_clusters.22, 23

visium <- FindNeighbors(
  visium, reduction = "pca", dims = dims.use
)
visium <- FindClusters(
  visium, resolution = 0.5, random.seed = 42
)

table(visium$seurat_clusters)

The graph in this workflow is built from gene expression, not spatial distances. Plotting its clusters on a tissue image does not make the clustering spatially constrained. Cluster numbers are also not cell-type annotations.

Run non-linear dimensional reduction#

We next run UMAP on the same PCs and color each point by its graph-based cluster. Nearby points have similar expression profiles in this representation. Distances between separate islands should not be interpreted as physical distances across the tissue.24

visium <- RunUMAP(
  visium,
  reduction = "pca",
  dims = dims.use,
  seed.use = 42
)

p.umap <- DimPlot(
  visium, reduction = "umap",
  group.by = "seurat_clusters", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE
)
p.tissue <- SpatialDimPlot(
  visium, images = "v1", group.by = "seurat_clusters",
  label = TRUE, label.size = 3
)
p.umap | p.tissue

The panels show the same assignments in two coordinate systems. The left panel is an expression embedding; the right panel preserves the tissue layout. We use both views to identify coherent anatomical patterns and to investigate unexpected groups.

The example retains all tissue-associated spots after the zero-information check. It is a worked clustering demonstration, not a final cell-type annotation or a claim that all spots have passed a study-specific QC policy.

Seurat’s default UMAP implementation uses the R package uwot. This workflow does not require switching reticulate to a Python environment.24

Repeat the workflow for Visium v2#

The v2/CytAssist data use the same spot-based Seurat interfaces. The biological preparation and molecular capture differ, but the count-to-PCA-to-UMAP operations do not become a different algorithm simply because the assay is labeled v2. We inspect its QC separately and fit normalization and feature selection to that sample.

For compactness, the function below collects the main-route steps above. It includes only the technical zero-information exclusion, so replace that selection with your documented sample-specific policy when analyzing your own data.

run_spot_workflow <- function(x, dims = 1:30, resolution = 0.5) {
  DefaultAssay(x) <- "Spatial"
  x$qc_keep <- x$nCount_Spatial > 0 & x$nFeature_Spatial >= 1
  x <- subset(x, subset = qc_keep)
  x <- NormalizeData(x, normalization.method = "LogNormalize", scale.factor = 10000)
  x <- FindVariableFeatures(x, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000)
  x <- ScaleData(x, features = VariableFeatures(x))
  x <- RunPCA(x, features = VariableFeatures(x), npcs = 50, seed.use = 42)
  x <- FindNeighbors(x, reduction = "pca", dims = dims)
  x <- FindClusters(x, resolution = resolution, random.seed = 42)
  x <- RunUMAP(x, reduction = "pca", dims = dims, seed.use = 42)
  x
}

VlnPlot(v2, features = c("nCount_Spatial", "nFeature_Spatial"), pt.size = 0)
SpatialFeaturePlot(v2, features = "nCount_Spatial", images = "v2")

v2 <- run_spot_workflow(v2)
DimPlot(v2, reduction = "umap", group.by = "seurat_clusters", label = TRUE) |
  SpatialDimPlot(v2, images = "v2", group.by = "seurat_clusters", label = TRUE)
Executed exampleTissue-associated spotsMedian counts / spotMedian genes / spotClusters
V12,69624,5116,01514
V22,31023,3346,736.515

These are two different tissue sections, with different section planes, preservation methods, and capture chemistries. The table and UMAPs demonstrate how to run the workflow; they are not a controlled comparison of platform sensitivity or accuracy. Separate UMAP layouts and cluster numbers cannot be matched by position or color alone.7, 8

Load Visium HD count matrices#

We now switch from spots to HD bins. We use a separate object and load only 8 µm bins, so that the observation unit remains explicit throughout the analysis. The raw barcoded squares are 2 × 2 µm, while 8 and 16 µm outputs aggregate neighboring squares. A bin is not an inferred cell.3

The data directory below is the Space Ranger outs/ directory containing binned_outputs/. Keep the image, scale factors, and Parquet coordinate files with the matrices. Do not pass binned_outputs/ itself and then ask the loader to add that level again.14, 5

stopifnot(packageVersion("Seurat") >= "5.1.0")
stopifnot(requireNamespace("hdf5r", quietly = TRUE))
stopifnot(requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE))

hd <- Load10X_Spatial(
  data.dir = "path/to/HD_sample/outs",
  bin.size = 8,
  slice = "HD"
)

full.assay <- "Spatial.008um"
full.image <- "HD.008um"
DefaultAssay(hd) <- full.assay

Assays(hd)
Images(hd)
stopifnot(all(Cells(hd[[full.assay]]) %in% Cells(hd[[full.image]])))

The assay name is Spatial.008um. If 16 µm bins are also loaded, their assay is Spatial.016um; they contain a different set of observations and should not be treated as extra measurements of identical cells.

The following HD code is an executable template, not a locally executed result. A public example is available from the 10x Visium HD mouse brain dataset. Its full binned archive is approximately 4.3 GiB, and is not downloaded as part of this HTML file.

Preprocess and sketch the HD bins#

First, we inspect count depth and detected genes in the tissue. Low counts can reflect low cellular density as well as technical quality. We use a nonzero-count check as a minimal technical starting point, then log-normalize and identify variable features.

VlnPlot(
  hd, features = c("nCount_Spatial.008um", "nFeature_Spatial.008um"),
  pt.size = 0
)
SpatialFeaturePlot(hd, features = "nCount_Spatial.008um", images = full.image)

qc <- hd[[]]
keep.bins <- rownames(qc)[qc$nCount_Spatial.008um > 0]
hd <- subset(hd, cells = keep.bins)

hd <- NormalizeData(hd, normalization.method = "LogNormalize", scale.factor = 10000)
hd <- FindVariableFeatures(hd, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000)

For a small dataset, the standard workflow can be applied directly. Large HD datasets often contain hundreds of thousands of bins, so we instead select a representative sketch. Leverage-score sampling is designed to preserve informative and less common expression patterns. It is not an additional spatial binning operation.11

hd <- SketchData(
  object = hd,
  assay = full.assay,
  ncells = min(50000L, ncol(hd[[full.assay]])),
  method = "LeverageScore",
  sketched.assay = "sketch",
  seed = 42
)

DefaultAssay(hd) <- "sketch"
hd <- FindVariableFeatures(hd, nfeatures = 2000)
hd <- ScaleData(hd, features = VariableFeatures(hd))
hd <- RunPCA(
  hd, assay = "sketch", features = VariableFeatures(hd),
  npcs = 50, reduction.name = "pca.sketch", seed.use = 42
)

ElbowPlot(hd, reduction = "pca.sketch", ndims = 50)
hd.dims <- 1:30

We normalize and select features on the full assay before sketching, but keep dense scaling and PCA on the sketch. This follows the generic sketch requirements and reduces the need to scale the entire in-memory dataset. The full count matrix still needs to fit the chosen storage approach; sketching alone does not make import memory-free.10

Cluster the sketch and project to all HD bins#

We perform the graph and UMAP steps on the sketch, retaining the fitted UMAP model. We then project the learned representation and cluster labels to all retained bins. This last step is important: a sketch-only UMAP is not a UMAP of the entire tissue.

hd <- FindNeighbors(
  hd, assay = "sketch", reduction = "pca.sketch", dims = hd.dims,
  graph.name = c("hd_sketch_nn", "hd_sketch_snn")
)
hd <- FindClusters(
  hd, graph.name = "hd_sketch_snn", cluster.name = "hd_cluster_sketch",
  resolution = 0.5, random.seed = 42
)
hd <- RunUMAP(
  hd, reduction = "pca.sketch", dims = hd.dims,
  reduction.name = "umap.sketch", return.model = TRUE, seed.use = 42
)

hd <- ProjectData(
  object = hd,
  assay = full.assay,
  full.reduction = "full.pca.sketch",
  sketched.assay = "sketch",
  sketched.reduction = "pca.sketch",
  umap.model = "umap.sketch",
  dims = hd.dims,
  refdata = list(hd_cluster_full = "hd_cluster_sketch")
)

return.model = TRUE supplies the UMAP model needed for projection. ProjectData() transfers labels from the sketch; it does not rerun independent graph clustering on every full-data bin.12

DefaultAssay(hd) <- full.assay
Idents(hd) <- "hd_cluster_full"
Reductions(hd)

p.hd.umap <- DimPlot(
  hd, reduction = "full.umap.sketch",
  group.by = "hd_cluster_full", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE
)
p.hd.tissue <- SpatialDimPlot(
  hd, images = full.image,
  group.by = "hd_cluster_full", label = TRUE, label.size = 3
)
p.hd.umap | p.hd.tissue
ResultWhere to find it
PCA learned on the sketchhd[["pca.sketch"]]
UMAP learned on the sketchhd[["umap.sketch"]]
PCA projected to all retained binshd[["full.pca.sketch"]]
UMAP projected to all retained binshd[["full.umap.sketch"]]
Transferred cluster labelshd$hd_cluster_full

The reduction names above match this fresh, sequential run. Inspect Reductions(hd) when rerunning projection on an existing object. This code produces both the projected UMAP and its tissue map; no simulated HD result is displayed here.

Analyze HD segmentation-derived cells#

If Space Ranger has generated cell segmentations, we can analyze their cell-level count matrix instead of fixed-size bins. We load a separate object containing the Spatial.Polygons assay. The cell boundaries are inferred from the image and the segmentation procedure; they still require inspection for missed cells, merged cells, and implausible expansion.4, 17

stopifnot(packageVersion("Seurat") >= "5.4.0")
stopifnot(packageVersion("SeuratObject") >= "5.3.0")
stopifnot(requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE))
stopifnot(requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE))

hd.cells <- Load10X_Spatial(
  data.dir = "path/to/HD_sample/outs",
  bin.size = "polygons",
  slice = "HD",
  image.name = "tissue_hires_image.png"
)
DefaultAssay(hd.cells) <- "Spatial.Polygons"
Assays(hd.cells)
Images(hd.cells)  # HD.polygons

We inspect cell-level counts and detected genes, and review the segmentation overlay on the tissue. The code below only excludes zero-count observations; it does not implement a complete segmentation QC policy.

VlnPlot(
  hd.cells,
  features = c("nCount_Spatial.Polygons", "nFeature_Spatial.Polygons"),
  pt.size = 0
)

qc.cells <- hd.cells[[]]
keep.cells <- rownames(qc.cells)[qc.cells$nCount_Spatial.Polygons > 0]
hd.cells <- subset(hd.cells, cells = keep.cells)

hd.cells <- NormalizeData(hd.cells, normalization.method = "LogNormalize", scale.factor = 10000)
hd.cells <- FindVariableFeatures(hd.cells, nfeatures = 2000)
hd.cells <- ScaleData(hd.cells, features = VariableFeatures(hd.cells))
hd.cells <- RunPCA(hd.cells, features = VariableFeatures(hd.cells), npcs = 50, seed.use = 42)

ElbowPlot(hd.cells, ndims = 50)
cell.dims <- 1:30
hd.cells <- FindNeighbors(hd.cells, reduction = "pca", dims = cell.dims)
hd.cells <- FindClusters(
  hd.cells, resolution = 0.5,
  cluster.name = "segmentation_clusters", random.seed = 42
)
hd.cells <- RunUMAP(hd.cells, reduction = "pca", dims = cell.dims, seed.use = 42)
p.cell.umap <- DimPlot(
  hd.cells, reduction = "umap",
  group.by = "segmentation_clusters", label = TRUE
)
p.cell.tissue <- SpatialDimPlot(
  hd.cells, images = "HD.polygons",
  group.by = "segmentation_clusters", plot_segmentations = TRUE
)
p.cell.umap | p.cell.tissue

This branch combines the documented polygon import with standard local Seurat clustering; it is not an automated annotation workflow. If the cell-level dataset is too large for dense scaling and PCA, apply the same sketch strategy to Spatial.Polygons. Bin-level and cell-level cluster labels are different partitions of different observations.

Interpreting and saving the results#

At this point, each branch has an expression-derived UMAP, cluster assignments, and a spatial view of those assignments. These are useful starting points, but a cluster number does not establish a cell type. Inspect marker expression and tissue morphology, and use an appropriate reference or validation strategy when assigning biological labels.

QuestionWhat to inspect
Does the cluster have a coherent expression profile?Marker genes and the normalized assay used for the analysis
Where does it occur in the tissue?SpatialDimPlot() and SpatialFeaturePlot()
Is it driven by technical quality?Counts, features, tissue mask, image alignment, and relevant assay QC
Is one point one cell?The selected spot / bin / segmented-cell observation unit
Can UMAP islands from separate samples be compared directly?Not by position or color; use a deliberately designed comparison or integration
# For the standard Visium object analyzed above:
saveRDS(visium, "visium_v1_processed.rds")
saveRDS(v2, "visium_v2_processed.rds")
write.csv(visium[[]], "visium_v1_metadata.csv")
write.csv(Embeddings(visium, reduction = "umap"), "visium_v1_umap.csv")

# Save the corresponding object separately after running an HD branch.
# saveRDS(hd, "visium_hd_bins_processed.rds")
# saveRDS(hd.cells, "visium_hd_cells_processed.rds")

Keep the original Space Ranger outputs, data provenance, chosen QC rules, feature selection, PC count, resolution, and random seed with the analysis. Do not merge v1, v2, and HD objects just to force a single UMAP before deciding what observations and biological effects should be compared.

Session Info#

The v1 and v2 figures were generated from the stated public datasets with the main LogNormalize workflow. HD code was checked against the current Seurat interfaces and parsed for syntax, but was not executed on a full HD dataset. No package installations or RStudio configuration changes were made.

Complete code files: standard Visium, HD bins and sketch projection, and HD segmented cells. The HD scripts contain placeholder data paths.

References#

Scientific content and function interfaces were checked against the official pages below on October 26, 2026. The article follows the visual conventions and guided teaching structure of the PBMC3k tutorial, with original text for these spatial workflows. It is an independent set of study notes.
